title: Query optimisation: plan search
lead: Single-table access, join-tree enumeration, dynamic programming and interesting orders.
goals: Interesting orders and final plan cost

sections.title: Single-table plan selection
sections.html:
Enumerating and comparing candidates

A logical query can use different access paths, join orders, join algorithms and memory allocations. The optimiser generates candidates, estimates their costs and chooses one. Exhaustive search may be impossible; a practical objective is avoiding disastrous plans within the allowed optimisation time. Single-table plans provide the base cases for multi-table search, including selection, projection, grouping and duplicate elimination.

PDF pp. 1–5

Single-table source example: 55, 4005 or 500

For a matching unique-key B+ tree, charge descent, the qualifying leaf entry and the heap fetch according to the source’s Height convention. For a matching non-unique predicate, its simplified estimates are (index pages+table pages)×sel when clustered and (index pages+table tuples)×sel when unclustered; always compare a scan and charge any required duplicate elimination.

Sailors has 40,000 tuples on 500 pages; rating has ten distinct values and its index has 50 pages. rating=8 estimates 4,000 rows. Clustered: (50+500)/10=55 I/Os. Unclustered: (50+40,000)/10=4,005. A file scan costs 500, so it beats this unclustered estimate. An index on sid does not restrict rating: traversing all of it costs about 550 clustered or 40,050 unclustered. These are teaching approximations; descent, caching and actual clustering alter measurements.

PDF pp. 6–7

sections.title: Join trees and restricted search
sections.html:
Combinatorial join search

A query block with n relations admits binary join trees and leaf permutations. The source counts below already explode before choosing hash, merge or nested loops and access paths.

Relations234567810
Join trees2121201,68030,240665,28017,297,28017,643,225,600

These counts include ordered binary trees, not merely n! left-deep relation orders. Distinguish the logical search space from the additional physical implementation choices.

PDF pp. 8–9

Why System R restricts the tree shape

A left-deep tree has a base relation as the right input at each join; a right-deep tree grows on the other side; a bushy tree may join two intermediate results. System R favours left-deep trees, enabling indexed inner probes and many pipelines. Blocking sorts still interrupt a left-deep pipeline, so tree shape alone does not guarantee streaming.

Enumerate physical joins and access paths inside the chosen tree family and normally discard Cartesian products. A disconnected query graph eventually requires a product; some unusual cost models can also make one useful. Modern optimisers can explore larger tree families.

PDF pp. 10–12

sections.title: Dynamic programming
sections.html:
Optimal substructure and pass one

Dynamic programming reuses subplans instead of costing the same subset repeatedly. For R,S,T, the best left-deep plan ends with one of best(RS) join T, best(RT) join S or best(ST) join R. This principle requires the retained state to include physical properties that affect later cost; an unordered cheapest subplan alone is insufficient.

In the source query R.A=S.A AND S.B=T.B, pass one compares scans/indexes for R, S and T. It does not join them yet. Each saved plan has an estimated cardinality, cost and useful output properties.

PDF pp. 13–14

Pass two: connected pairs

Build both orientations of R join S on A and S join T on B. Compare hash and sort-merge implementations, input access paths and any sort costs. R join T has no direct predicate in this example, so normal Cartesian-product pruning removes it. The progressive source figures first display alternatives, then retain the best candidates; they do not supply numerical costs from which a new numeric winner can be reconstructed.

PDF pp. 15–16

Pass three: extend the saved pairs

Extend the RS candidate with T using S.B=T.B, and the ST candidate with R using S.A=R.A. Consider alternative final join methods, estimate total cost including the saved subplan and discard inferior alternatives. The last source figure retains a plan joining T and S with hash join and then R with sort-merge. Its role is to illustrate successive enumeration and pruning, not to claim those methods always win.

A useful recurrence is C[S,p]=min(C[S minus {T},q]+access(T,a)+joinCost(q,a→p)), over allowed T, access paths a and input properties q. Include required enforcers such as sorting. Increasing subset size makes every referenced smaller state available.

PDF pp. 17–19

sections.title: Interesting orders and final plan cost
sections.html:
Interesting orders

A slightly more expensive sorted subplan can avoid a later sort for merge join, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or ORDER BY. For each relation subset, retain the cheapest plan overall and the cheapest plan for each relevant interesting order. Orders come from query requirements and subsequent join attributes. This is how property-aware states repair a naive “one cheapest plan per subset” algorithm.

PDF p. 20

Three-table example through final aggregation

The source joins Sailors S, Reserves R and Boats B, filters B.color='red' and groups by S.sid to count reservations. Access paths are S.sid B+ tree; clustered R.bid and unclustered R.sid trees; B.color tree. Pass one keeps scans for S,R, a color-index selection for B, plus interesting ordered alternatives S.sid,R.bid,R.sid.

Pass two extends each saved plan with each missing table, each access method and each join method; remove products and keep cheapest plans per (subset,order). Pass three repeats. The illustrated candidate merges selected Boats with Reserves on bid, then index-nested-loops into Sailors on sid. Ordering by bid helps that merge but does not supply the final sid grouping order. Add group-by/aggregate cost, including a sort by sid unless an existing operator already supplies it; only then choose the cheapest complete plan. Search quality depends jointly on enumeration, cardinality estimates, operator costs and property tracking.

PDF pp. 21–24

quiz.question: Why retain a more expensive subplan that already produces sorted output?
options: Because sorted output is always better
Because it may avoid an expensive sort later
Because subplan cost does not matter
quiz.explanation: An interesting order can reduce the total plan cost by avoiding a later sort, even if that subplan costs more.

Topics covered: Single-table access enumeration and cost; Join-tree combinatorial growth; Left-deep versus bushy/right-deep; Cross-product pruning; Dynamic programming and optimal substructure; Interesting orders and property-aware retention; Final grouping/sorting cost.
